verdict.reasoning: Patient reports cough and runny nose starting “maybe a bit less than a week ago. Like, maybe five or six days ago” and earlier says “this, like, cough for quite a few days, and my nose is running”.
Patient says “It's just so continuous… It's quite dry and it's just all day. Like, keeps me up at night as well,” and confirms not bringing up phlegm: “You don't bring up any mucky phlegm… No, no.”
Patient: “the coughing is giving me a sore throat… Just my throat is irritated from coughing, but it's not like… it's not that bad when I swallow or anything.”
Rhinorrhea = runny nose. Patient: “my nose is running” and clinician: “You mentioned a bit of a runny nose. Right? – Yeah.”
Patient: “I've been having, like, shivers even when I'm in bed… I just, like, couldn't stop shivering.”
Patient: “I haven't taken my Temperature. So I'm not 100% sure if I had a fever, but feels like I probably did.” This is a subjective fever without a recorded temperature.
Patient: “my muscle was really hurting… Especially, like, in my arms, my legs, like, just everywhere.” Myalgias affecting arms and legs are described.
Patient: “I feel, you know, generally tired.”
Clinician: “Basically getting quite lethargic and weak. Mentioned.” Patient: “Yeah, pretty much.”

Patient had diarrhea at onset that resolved: “at the beginning… I had a little bit of diarrhea… Has it got better now…? – Yeah, yeah, it got better… it started at the same time as the cough… and then it stopped.”
Clinician: “You don't feel breathless, do you?” Patient: “I don't feel breathless, no.”
Clinician: “Any pain in your chest?” Patient: “No, not that either.”
Ears: “Your ears feel blocked? – No, they feel okay… No pain or discharge? – Not pain on the ears?” indicating no ear pain or blockage.
Clinician: “have you had any nausea? Have you had any vomiting?” Patient: “No, no. No nausea, no vomiting.”
Urinary: “Any problems with your waterworks at all?… – Oh, no, no, no. That's fine.”

Clinician asks about “Any funny skin rashes,” but the patient’s answer focuses on muscle pain: “my muscle was really hurting.” She does not explicitly deny rash, so documenting “denies rash” adds information not stated.
Patient: “Well, I have type 2 diabetes.”
Patient: “I have quite high blood pressure.”
Patient: “I take Metformin for the diabetes.”
Patient: “And I take Lisinopril for the high blood pressure.”
Clinician: “Any allergies at all to medication?” Patient: “No allergies, no.”
Patient: “My dad also has type 2 diabetes.”
Social: “who lives at home with you? – Just. It's just me and my partner.”
Work: “What is it that you do for work? – I am a developer. – So you work in the IT field.”
Smoking: “Do you smoke at all, April? – I used to, but I've stopped for about six months now.”
Alcohol: patient drinks wine “three evenings a week” and “maybe two or three glasses” per evening.
The transcript contains no mention of vital signs or any physical examination; stating none are documented correctly reflects their absence.

Clinician assessment: “I think… you're going through a bit of a viral illness” and may consider antibiotics later. No explicit differential of “viral upper respiratory tract infection versus early lower respiratory tract infection” or mention of “no red-flag features.”
Diabetes control status is described only by patient: “I have it under control… regularly checking that it's under control.” The clinician does not formally assess it as stable on Metformin.
Similarly, patient says blood pressure is under control, but clinician does not explicitly assess “Hypertension… controlled on Lisinopril.” This is an added assessment.

Clinician characterizes intake relative to guidelines: “So… you're probably just about under the limit of the recommended limit… maybe something that you can maybe cut down on.” This reflects moderate alcohol use.
Recent cessation is documented: “I used to [smoke], but I've stopped for about six months now.”
Advice: “things you can do to help yourself in the meantime is to get some nice rest.”
Advice: “drink plenty of fluids, keep yourself well hydrated.”
Advice: “You can take regular paracetamol.”
Work advice: “maybe take a day or two off work if you can get some good bed rest, and maybe think about work early next week.”

Clinician: “If you feel like it's still any better in two to three days, it's probably worth coming back… if you are still feeling feverish and your cough isn't getting any better, then we may look to give you some antibiotics for your chest.” No mention of fever >3 days, dyspnea, symptoms >10 days, or chest X-ray; those triggers and imaging are added and conflict with the actual follow-up criteria.
There is no explicit plan statement like “continue Metformin” in the transcript; medications are listed but no ongoing management instruction is given.

While diabetes follow-up is mentioned historically (“I just regularly go see a doctor that just checks up on it”), no new or specific recommendation for routine PCP follow-up is made in this encounter.
Lisinopril is listed but the clinician does not explicitly instruct the patient to “continue Lisinopril.”
The transcript mentions the patient has been “regularly checking” blood pressure but no new recommendation is made for routine BP checks in the plan.

Counseling: “maybe… cut down to two glasses a week and then one week thereafter. And if you are coping okay, then we can maybe try and cut down altogether,” i.e., reduce to ≤2 glasses/week with goal of abstinence.
Smoking cessation is noted but there is no counseling or offer of support resources: no advice or resources are discussed.

Stated follow-up: return “if you feel like it's still any better in two to three days,” and earlier return “if your cough isn't getting any better or your breathing is getting worse.” No mention of fever >3 days, symptoms >10 days, or specific duration thresholds; the detailed criteria in the fact go beyond and differ from what was said.
Ongoing diabetes care is described historically but no explicit new “routine primary care follow-up” plan is made during this visit.
